content:
In the past few days, two reports have highlighted different ways Apple is boosting profits by increasing services revenue.

Apple should absolutely pursue the first approach in my view, but not the second — and it looks like Phil Schiller may agree…

Let me first summarize the two reports.

Home security and monitoring services

On Friday, a Bloomberg report said Apple is potentially planning to launch a brand-new home security and monitoring service, rolling out alongside some of the new home hardware we're expecting.

Squeezing more revenue from the App Store

The second report, from the same source on Sunday, said Apple is exploring ways to squeeze more revenue and profit from the App Store.

Apple should not pursue the latter approach

Speaking in reverse order, I think the second approach would be a very big mistake.

Apple's effective monopoly position on iPhone app sales has come under fierce criticism from regulators around the world. In most countries, if you want to sell an iPhone app, you're forced to do so through the official App Store, leaving you with no choice but to accept Apple's terms — take it or leave it.

I know there's a common view that no one is forced to buy an iPhone or develop apps for it, but that doesn't match how even the most laissez-faire capitalism works in practice: even in the US, antitrust laws have been in place since 1890. When you reach a certain level of market dominance, you become subject to conduct requirements to ensure you don't abuse that position.

Trying to extract more money from the App Store is the exact opposite of "skating to where the puck is going" — and reportedly Schiller himself agrees, with Bloomberg saying it's one of the reasons for him stepping back now.

Innovative services are the right direction

In contrast, launching innovative new services people actually want to buy is the right direction for Apple. I can easily see the value in Apple offering a home security monitoring service.

I said way back in 2024 that making its own smart home cameras would be one of the smartest moves Apple could make. I've said the same about rumored smart doorbells. Adding an optional service package to security products is an entirely sensible move, for two reasons.

First, for all the privacy reasons I've mentioned before. HomeKit Secure Video already does a great deal to protect the privacy of security camera footage. If there's one company I'd trust to take my security camera footage and run AI analysis on it, it's Apple.

Second, Apple is best placed to fully integrate security hardware and services within the HomeKit ecosystem. I'm sure there are many other areas in which Apple could offer similar benefits.

For me, the key point is that Apple needs to take the same approach with services as it does with hardware. Make great products that people willingly and happily pay for — not extract money in ways that annoy customers, developers, and regulators.

What do you think? Share your views in the comments section.
